name: David Foster Wallace
essay: And but so the real genius of the recurring auto-debit fitness subscription—the digital phantom keycard you keep tucked inside your phone’s dark wallet—is that it does not charge you for access to heavy objects, exactly, but rather sells you a monthly indulgence for the crime of remaining yourself. Which is to say that every time the automated micro-charge hits your statement, silent as a heart attack in a clean sweater, you experience a tiny, exquisite flash of moral absolution, because paying for the possibility of sweat feels, to the modern neurosis, functionally identical to sweating itself. You tell yourself you’ll go Tuesday—or at least stream the thirty-minute high-intensity interval session while your pasta boils—even though you know, deep down in the soggy, un-toned center of your being, that the app’s sleek little icon exists now purely as a tiny, purple monument to your own ambient dread. And so you keep paying the twelve dollars, month after month, not out of hope, but because canceling it would require a level of brutal, unmediated honesty about your actual physical future that I, personally, am entirely unprepared to face.

name: Ambrose Bierce
essay: PNEUMATIC DRYER, n. An acoustic terror of public lavatories, devised by mechanical ingenuity to replace the quiet efficacy of the linen towel with thirty seconds of gale-force turbulence and the ultimate necessity of wiping one's wet palms upon one's trousers. It operates by means of an invisible sensor that detects human presence only after an agonizing period of frantic gesticulation, whereupon it releases a warm, tempestuous blast calculated to scatter moisture from the skin into the surrounding atmosphere, whence it may be inhaled by the helpless bystander. The machine is acclaimed by municipal economists as a supreme triumph of thrift, since it consumes only electricity, public patience, and the hearing of its victim, while leaving the hands precisely as damp as they were before the tempest commenced, though considerably colder and less clean. Thus does modern civilization demonstrate its relentless march: by substituting a deafening clamor for a silent cloth, so that he who sought merely to dry his fingers is returned to society with his dignity diminished, his ears ringing, and his own coat stealthily recruited to fulfill the ancient purpose of the towel.

name: Dorothy Parker
essay: They ask if my experience was delightful, as though buying a turnip were a weekend in Capri. There are five little boxes to check, ranging from 'Strongly Agree' to a quiet, dignified despair. I am invited to rate the enthusiasm of a young man named Kevin, whose devotion to my dry-cleaning was apparently meant to alter my soul. I gave him five stars, because I have seen what happens to boys who fail to charm the public, and most of them end up writing poetry. The manager hopes I will take two minutes to describe my journey. My journey consisted of standing near the umbrella rack while rain ruined my coat and a clerk explained the refund policy to a weeping woman. I am told my opinion is invaluable, which is the word people use when they mean free. They wish to know if I felt valued as a patron. I felt like a hostage who had been handed a receipt. If I rate their helpfulness as merely adequate, someone in Ohio will be forced to attend a seminar. I answered every question with the frantic praise of a convict negotiating parole. I hope Kevin gets his promotion. I shall never go back.

name: George Orwell
essay: The door shuts with a soft rubber click, and the click is what matters. No one asked for a box that counts your eggs, but it is easier to let the box remember than to remember yourself. Inside, a cold light sits upon the butter like a small eye. It tells you the milk is sour before you have smelled it, and it orders a fresh bottle before you have felt the urge to drink. That is the whole trick of the modern machine. It does not force a man to obey; it simply takes the trouble of choosing off his hands. A citizen who leaves his breakfast to an engine will soon leave his conscience there as well, though he will swear he bought the thing for quietness and ease. Ease is the cleanest way to break a mind. When the white cabinet hums in the corner, keeping its quiet count of your lard and cheese, it is not keeping your house in order. It is keeping you in order. You give up the right to be hungry on your own terms for the cheap comfort of a full shelf. One day we shall wake up and find we have forgotten how to want.

name: David Foster Wallace
essay: And but so the weirdly profound violence of the little square box—the one you are meant to check, unthinkingly, after scrolling through sixteen thousand words of unreadable legalese designed by corporate attorneys whose whole career trajectory depends on your total refusal to read it—is that it converts an act of complete, desperate surrender into a tiny gesture of personal agency. Which is to say that by clicking it, you are not merely agreeing to let a distant server harvest your biometric telemetry or whatever; you are participating in a quiet, modern form of perjury where everybody involved knows you are lying, and knows that you know you are lying, but the checkbox exists precisely to give your dishonesty a neat, digital border. You click it because you want the video to play, or the app to open, or the dopamine to hit, but mostly because the alternative—which would be standing on the moral principle of actually reading the document—requires a level of existential stamina that neither you nor I possess. And so you check it, and in doing so, you realize that the box was never really a contract at all, but a tiny, mirrored tile reflecting the exact dimension of my own comfortable, eager compliance.

name: Dorothy Parker
essay: They told me this little glowing square would streamline my existence, which is the phrase people use when they intend to make your life entirely unendurable. It buzzes on the nightstand every morning at seven to remind me to breathe, as if I had been managing the business until now purely by accident. There is a cheerful pink circle that turns green whenever I accomplish a task, such as drinking water or resisting the urge to throw myself down the stairs. I spent three full hours yesterday color-coding my failures into neat little categories marked Urgent and Low Priority. It keeps a meticulous record of my habits, though it stubbornly refuses to log my primary daily activity, which is staring at the ceiling while waiting for lunch. At noon, a polite chime informed me that I was eighty percent optimized for joy. I have experienced warmer jubilation in a dentist's waiting room. Still, I dutifully clear the tiny red flags, pretending an algorithm can repair a heart that was thoroughly broken long before the battery was charged. Tonight it asked me to rate my evening on a scale of one to five stars. I gave it two, which was generous considering I spent it alone.
